chunks: Active probe and when to use one. The question: What is an active probe? When do I need it?
An active probe has a tiny amplifier at its tip. The amplifier barely loads the circuit, so it adds very little capacitance to the node.
A standard passive 10x probe adds about 10 to 15 picofarads. An active probe adds about 1 picofarads or less.
Capacitance is like a small bucket that must fill before the voltage on a wire can rise. A passive probe adds a bigger bucket to the node.
A weak driver needs longer to fill it, so the edge slows. An active probe adds only a thimble. The limit: its amplifier handles only a few volts and breaks more easily.
The passive probe starts higher but loses to the active probe above roughly 10 kilohertz and keeps falling at 20 decibels per decade.
Near 100 megahertz the passive is about 130 ohms (a loud load for a 500 ohms node) while the active is still about 1. 6 kilohms.
The crossing with the 500 ohms line marks where each probe starts to load a 500 ohms node heavily.
Capacitance: how much charge a part must take in for its voltage to rise. A pF is a trillionth of a farad. Passive probe: a plain probe of wire and resistors with no amplifier.
A 10x passive probe has about 10 megohms in parallel with 10 to 15 picofarads. Source impedance: the resistance a node drives through. A high one is easy to disturb.
Rise time: the time an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of its final value.
A node is driven through 500 ohms and has a fast, clean 1 nanoseconds edge. Add a passive probe with 12 picofarads.
The 500 ohms and the probe capacitance slow the edge, which now takes about 2. 2 times 500 times 12 picofarads equals 13 nanoseconds. The probe has changed what you are measuring.
Now use an active probe with 1 picofarads. It adds only about 2. 2 times 500 times 1 picofarads equals 1. 1 nanoseconds of its own, so the edge stays near 1. 5 nanoseconds.
At 100 megahertz the 12 picofarads probe acts like a 133 ohms load, heavy on a 500 ohms node. The 1 picofarads probe acts like 1. 6 kilohms. That is the whole idea.
"An active probe has a small buffer amplifier at the tip, so it has high resistance and very low input capacitance, around a picofarad, versus 10 to 15 picofarads for a passive 10x.
That means much less loading at high frequency, so I use it for fast edges, clocks, high-speed buses and sensitive high-impedance nodes.
The costs are price, limited voltage range, noise, fragility and needing power from the scope."
